title: Efficient creation of shallow NV$^-$ ensembles by high-angle ion implantation
authors: Kento Sasaki, Hideyuki Watanabe, Tokuyuki Teraji, Takashi Taniguchi, Kenji Watanabe, Kensuke Kobayashi
abstract: Negatively charged nitrogen-vacancy (NV$^-$) centers located a few nanometers below the diamond surface are key quantum defects for nanoscale sensing of external spins. However, the creation of shallow NV$^-$ centers with high yield remains a materials challenge. Here, we demonstrate that high-angle ion implantation enhances the creation efficiency of shallow NV$^-$ centers. By implanting $^{15}$N ions at angles exceeding 60$^\circ$, we achieve high NV$^-$ yields approaching 10% with effective NV$^-$ depths below 10 nm. These yields are significantly higher than those typically reported for shallow NV$^-$ creation. The enhanced NV$^-$ yield is consistent with an increased vacancy-to-nitrogen ratio in the near-surface region, which is expected to promote NV formation during annealing. The created NV$^-$ ensembles show coherence properties comparable to those of single shallow NV$^-$ centers at similar depths, and allow detection of nuclear spins in van der Waals materials attached to the diamond surface. Our results establish geometric control of ion implantation as a simple and broadly applicable approach to engineer shallow vacancy-related quantum defects.
summary: This paper demonstrates that using high-angle ion implantation is an effective, simple, and scalable method to create high-yield ensembles of shallow nitrogen-vacancy ($	ext{NV}^-$) centers in diamond. By controlling the ion incidence angle, the authors manipulate the near-surface vacancy concentration, leading to superior quantum defect quality and depth control compared to conventional methods.
main_problem: The primary challenge is the efficient creation of shallow, high-yield negatively charged nitrogen-vacancy ($	ext{NV}^-$) ensembles in diamond for nanoscale quantum sensing.
main_result: High-angle ion implantation ($	ext{N}$ ions at angles $>60^\circ$) significantly enhances $	ext{NV}^-$ yields (approaching 10%) and allows for the engineering of shallow $	ext{NV}^-$ depths ($<10 	ext{ nm}$) in a simple, mask-free manner.
method: The authors used high-angle ion implantation of ${}^{15}	ext{N}$ ions into diamond, followed by thermal annealing, and characterized the resulting quantum defects using confocal photoluminescence (PL) microscopy and time-resolved spin measurements.
model_or_system: The physical system is $	ext{NV}^-$ centers embedded in diamond. The method relies on the geometric control afforded by oblique ion incidence, which alters the near-surface vacancy-to-nitrogen ratio, promoting $	ext{NV}$ formation.
key_observables: Photoluminescence (PL) intensity, PL spectra (Zero-Phonon Line at 637 nm), $	ext{NV}^-$ ensemble depth ($d_{	ext{nv}}$), spin coherence time ($T_2$), and $	ext{NV}^-$ yield.
important_parameters: Implantation angle ($	heta > 60^\circ$), ion energy (5 keV), and the resulting vacancy-to-nitrogen ratio.
main_assumptions: The PL signals are assumed to originate predominantly from charge-stable $	ext{NV}^-$ centers, and the technique is proposed as a general method for engineering shallow vacancy-related defects.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the dependence of PL intensity and $	ext{NV}^-$ yield on implantation angle, and show PL maps and spectra confirming the enhanced yield and coherence properties at high angles.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem of shallow $	ext{NV}^-$ creation, proposes high-angle ion implantation as a solution, details the experimental characterization (PL, spin measurements), and concludes by demonstrating the superior performance and applicability of this geometric control method.
why_interesting: This work provides a highly practical, materials-engineering approach to creating quantum defects, which is crucial for realizing solid-state quantum sensors and quantum computing platforms.
